item.title: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that autonomously handle tasks and integrate with over 4,000 apps across Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced Dots, always-on AI agents designed to work continuously on users' behalf by learning preferences and managing tasks autonomously. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, these agents operate on their own cloud computers, connect to thousands of apps, and are accessible via platforms like ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams. Users can customize their primary Dot and expect future expansions to team-based and specialist Dots with deeper organizational integrations. Dots can independently manage projects, update work based on feedback, and assist across various roles such as development, product launches, research, sales, and content creation. Early examples include automating bug fixes, revising launch materials, updating scientific analyses, and preparing sales proposals. OpenAI is rolling out Dots to eligible markets and plans broader availability soon, aiming to enhance productivity by having AI agents continuously support users' goals and workflows.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol, matching GPT-6 Astra's intelligence on coding and professional tasks at one-fifth the token cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgrade to GPT-6 Sol that delivers near-GPT-6 Astra intelligence for agentic coding, computer use, and professional workflows at significantly reduced input and output token prices. The model offers substantial improvements in complex tasks such as software engineering, document understanding, and multi-step business workflows while reducing costs by up to 80% compared to Astra and 50% compared to GPT-6 Sol's cached input pricing. GPT-6.1 Sol outperforms previous versions on benchmarks including DeepSWE for coding, GDP.pdf for professional document analysis, AutomationBench for business workflows, OSWorld for computer-use tasks, and Terminal-Bench Science for scientific research workflows. It also improves factual accuracy on difficult prompts, reducing errors by about 32% at low reasoning effort compared to GPT-6 Sol. The model provides a cost-effective option for developers building capable AI agents across various professional domains.

item.title: Researchers find dominant language model supplier slows recursive drift more than steering it in multi-generation retraining experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers retrained eight open language models over five generations using a shared corpus with varying proportions of text from one dominant model, Phi-2, to study how it influences model drift. They found that while the models collectively drift toward a style with fewer function words, increasing Phi-2's share mainly delays the drift rather than steering other models toward its style, with significant delay observed when Phi-2 contributed 90% of the text. Other models contributing half the corpus slowed the ecosystem less or not at all, and human-written text also slowed drift along the same trajectory.

item.title: Researchers propose Decision-Sufficient State Representations to reduce write-time regret in LLM agents by training writers to optimize short written states for long tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Large language model (LLM) agents face challenges in managing long task histories that exceed their context capacity, leading to reliance on short written states rewritten at each step. This approach risks losing important information before it is needed, causing performance loss termed write-time regret. Researchers quantify this loss by comparing the written state to an optimal hindsight state and find that most loss arises from writer choices rather than inherent state size limitations. They introduce Decision-Sufficient State Representations (DSSR), a training method that scores candidate states based on how well the reader acts after the writer updates them, improving writer decisions and reducing regret. Experiments in TextWorld cooking games show that DSSR training increases success rates by up to 7 points when facts are needed soon, though gains diminish with longer delays due to credit assignment challenges in maintaining facts across rewrites.

item.title: Researchers find that fixed sampling seeds in recursive language model training cause rapid loss of lexical diversity due to replayed sampling noise [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers studied how language models degrade when trained on their own outputs, finding that fixed sampling seeds in the vLLM framework cause repeated random draws across requests and generations. This replayed sampling noise amplifies favored tokens during fine-tuning, leading to a rapid decline in lexical diversity within a few generations. Adjusting the sampling seeds to vary across requests or generations preserves diversity, while fixed seeds cause phrase repetition and model collapse in some cases. The study analyzed multiple StableLM checkpoints and a peer-reviewed Gemma-2-27B pipeline, showing that diversity loss is linked to the interaction of shared seeds across requests and replay across generations.

item.title: Multimodal LLMs outperform specialized pathology foundation models in cross-domain histological similarity across multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers found that general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) consistently outperform state-of-the-art pathology foundation models in judging histological similarity across different slides and institutions. Using the MOSAIC benchmark, they evaluated 17 models on six datasets and discovered that pathology encoders often misclassify tissue similarity by ranking same-institution, different-disease samples as more similar than same-disease, different-institution samples, a failure not detected by standard evaluations. The study suggests that LLMs' semantic visual comparison of morphology and tissue architecture makes them less prone to this error, whereas pathology models rely on shortcut features tied to acquisition context. Increasing training data did not fix this issue for pathology encoders, indicating the problem lies in the learning objectives. These findings reveal a robustness gap in current pathology models and position multimodal LLMs as promising alternatives for cross-institutional retrieval, dataset harmonization, and quality control in multi-site pathology workflows.

item.title: Researchers present a data-free sensitivity estimator using a single random Gaussian probe for mixed-precision quantization, achieving efficient bit allocation without calibration data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that a single random Gaussian probe can unbiasedly estimate the squared Frobenius norm of a layer's quantization error due to the spectrally flat nature of round-to-nearest error. This method accurately measures per-tensor sensitivity across various bit-widths and models, including a 35B MoE and a 9B dense model, with predictable variation based on tensor shape. The team applies this estimator in a budget-targeted mixed-precision quantization approach called RAM, which uses Gaussian probes carrying the network's input statistics to score tensors at six bit-widths. A knapsack solver then allocates bits under an exact byte budget, preventing poor 2-bit assignments. This approach performs competitively or better than existing methods across multiple architectures, reducing median WikiText-2 perplexity by 3.5 to 13.6% compared to uniform 4-bit quantization on tested MoE models, with probe timing scalable up to a 400B parameter model on a single workstation.

item.title: Adaptive Consistency Graph improves long-horizon decision-making in GPT-5.6-luna by organizing execution evidence into a persistent graph, boosting success rates from 44.5% to 50.2% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Large language model agents often struggle with tasks requiring long sequences of dependent actions, as task requirements and execution states can become disconnected over time. The Adaptive Consistency Graph (ACG) addresses this by incrementally organizing execution evidence and its provenance into a persistent graph, creating a requirement-centered context for each decision without replacing the base agent's planner or executor. In evaluations, ACG improved GPT-5.6-luna's average success rate from 44.5% to 50.2%, with the largest gain on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, rising from 62.4% to 73.5%. The study also analyzes trajectory structure and inference costs to explain these improvements, and the code has been made publicly available.

item.title: Researchers analyze transfer of corrected agent experience in AI tasks, finding mixed gains across 3,300 runs with ThinkingBox and APEX frameworks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This study investigates whether repairing a failed episode improves its usefulness as memory for subsequent AI tasks by transferring experiences before and after repair to a fixed target alongside independent execution. The experiments cover 3,300 runs across 100 ThinkingBox and 100 APEX task pairs under various conditions, revealing that ThinkingBox's correction methods yield significant performance gains over independence, while APEX shows no comparable aggregate benefits. The findings highlight that the value of repairing experience differs from simply reusing it, requiring both a reference to the previous version and a fresh start for effective memory updates.

item.title: Researchers present OmniTide, an algorithm-system co-design for efficient on-device streaming omni-modal LLM inference that reduces memory fragmentation and improves speed and accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OmniTide addresses the challenge of continuous multimodal data inflow exhausting memory and compute budgets in on-device streaming inference by combining algorithmic and system-level innovations. It uses modality-aware structural sparsity with OmniPick to retain critical context and OmniPage to partition and compact cache, minimizing fragmentation and overhead. Evaluations on multiple benchmarks and consumer devices show OmniTide achieves up to 12.72 times kernel speedups, 2.4 times lower latency, and up to 18 percentage points accuracy improvement over sliding-window baselines. OmniPage also reduces physical key-value cache span by up to 26.7%, enabling real-time infinite-context streaming on edge devices.

item.title: Researchers propose ReCommit, a diffusion-guided hierarchical search framework to improve tool-agent repair efficiency and recovery in large language model-driven tool use [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Tool agents that use large language models to operate external tools can still fail to fulfill user requests despite successful tool calls. Researchers introduce ReCommit, a training-free, diffusion-guided framework that formulates repair as a hierarchical search over operation supports to reduce costly regeneration and improve failure recovery. ReCommit reuses operation-type scores from a single masked diffusion language model readout to guide search across operation types while exploring alternative realizations within each support. Experiments on real failures across four enterprise services in the Agent-Diff benchmark demonstrate that ReCommit achieves up to 75.9% relative recovery gains and reduces mean repair time by over 50% compared to the strongest 8B parameter baseline, also showing favorable trade-offs against larger 32B models. This approach offers a more efficient method for tool-agent repair by balancing exploration of alternative operations and realizations while minimizing redundant computation.

item.title: Researchers propose a framework for fully connected and convolutional layers on Riemannian manifolds, covering ten manifold types including hyperbolic, SPD, and Grassmannian geometries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a framework to construct fully connected and convolutional neural network layers over computationally tractable Riemannian manifolds, generalizing Euclidean layers to non-Euclidean geometries. This approach unifies several previous methods as special cases and is demonstrated on ten representative manifolds, including three hyperbolic models, five symmetric positive definite (SPD) geometries, and two Grassmannian perspectives. Experiments show the framework's effectiveness across different manifolds, and the code has been made publicly available.

item.title: Researchers introduce MGSM-Pro for robust multilingual mathematical reasoning evaluation, revealing performance drops in low-resource languages and varying model robustness across nine languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed MGSM-Pro, an extension of the MGSM dataset using the GSM-Symbolic approach, to evaluate mathematical reasoning in large language models across nine languages. The dataset includes five variations per question by changing names, digits, and irrelevant context to test model robustness beyond English benchmarks. Evaluations show significant performance declines in low-resource languages when digit instantiations differ from the original test set, and robustness in high-resource languages does not always translate to low-resource ones. Proprietary models like Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4.1 exhibit less robustness to digit changes, while Gemini 3.0 Pro, GPT-OSS 120B, and DeepSeek v3 demonstrate stronger resilience. The study recommends using multiple digit-varying instantiations per problem for more reliable math reasoning assessments.

item.title: Researchers propose a set-valued set function model for dynamical grammatical gender shifting in noun morphology, demonstrating its application to lexical changes in Riffian
item.description: This study introduces a computational model based on a set-valued set function to predict nonlinear mappings of lexical items onto morphological templates, aiming to explain grammatical gender shifts and other morphosyntactic variations in nouns. The model, called the Template-Based and Modular Cognitive model, provides a unified framework for understanding morphological markings across languages and is empirically tested on Riffian lexical changes. The research formally proves the model's representational completeness and challenges traditional views of word formation by showing that noun-to-noun derivation through conversion is formally applicable, offering insights into morphosyntactic variation and potential applications in linguistic pattern modeling.

item.title: SalamahBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating safety of Arabic language models across dialects and harm categories with 49,620 harmful prompt instances [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: SalamahBench presents a unified benchmark to assess safety in Arabic language models (ALMs) by including 8,270 human-verified harmful prompts rendered in Modern Standard Arabic and five regional dialects, totaling 49,620 paired instances. The benchmark addresses the lack of fine-grained safety evaluation in Arabic NLP systems, which has hindered ALM adoption due to reliance on English-centric and standardized Arabic benchmarks. The study introduces metrics like Dialect Shift and Category-Specific Dialect Deviation to analyze model safety variations across dialects and harm categories. Evaluations of models such as Fanar 2, ALLaM 2, and Karnak 1 reveal that robustness varies significantly by model and that aggregate safety scores can mask category-level differences. The findings emphasize the importance of evaluating Arabic language model safety across multiple dialects and harm domains rather than relying solely on aggregate scores or Modern Standard Arabic.

item.title: SymDrift introduces symmetry-aware one-shot generative modeling for physical systems, reducing computational cost by up to 40 times compared to multi-step methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: SymDrift is a new framework for generative modeling of physical systems like molecules that respects global symmetries such as 3D rotations. It addresses a key challenge in drifting models, which struggle to produce consistent drifting fields under symmetry transformations, by making the drifting field itself symmetry-aware through symmetrized drift and invariant embeddings. The approach outperforms existing one-shot methods on benchmarks for conformer and transition state generation while remaining competitive with more expensive multi-step models. By enabling efficient one-shot inference, SymDrift significantly lowers computational overhead, making it suitable for applications like virtual drug screening and large-scale reaction network exploration.

item.title: CRAX benchmark accelerates safe reinforcement learning training up to 200x using MuJoCo XLA engine with eight tasks across difficulty levels [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CRAX (Constrained RL Accelerated with JAX) is a new benchmark designed to speed up safe reinforcement learning (RL) experiments, addressing the computational slowness of existing 3D physics-based safety benchmarks. Built on the MuJoCo XLA physics engine, CRAX uses vectorized operations and hardware acceleration to achieve up to 200 times faster training compared to CPU-based benchmarks, featuring eight tasks with varying difficulty and agent morphologies. The benchmark evaluated seven popular safe RL methods and found no single method dominates across all tasks, highlighting ongoing challenges in learning safe policies, especially from pixel inputs. CRAX aims to facilitate large-scale experimentation and rapid prototyping in safety-critical RL domains such as robotics and autonomous driving.

item.title: Jet-Long introduces a tuning-free zero-shot method for efficient long-context extension in LLMs using dynamic bifocal RoPE, improving accuracy and throughput up to 128K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Jet-Long is a new zero-shot method designed to extend the context length of large language models (LLMs) efficiently without retraining. It combines a local RoPE-faithful window with a dynamically adapting long-range window, allowing the model to maintain fidelity on short inputs while scaling cleanly to very long contexts, up to 128K tokens. This approach outperforms existing methods in benchmarks such as HELMET-RAG and PG-19 perplexity, and achieves high throughput on hardware like the H100 GPU. The method uses an inclusion-exclusion attention merge and on-the-fly RoPE correction to enable efficient implementation with CuTe. Evaluations on Qwen3 models of various sizes show Jet-Long leads prior baselines by several percentage points in accuracy and matches or exceeds throughput compared to FlashAttention-3. Additional tests on Meta-Llama-3-8B and hybrid architectures demonstrate the approach's broad applicability and robustness without requiring model retraining or tuning of local-window hyperparameters.

item.title: Researchers propose Cross-Variable Loss to improve multivariate time series forecasting by addressing dependencies among future variables [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Multivariate time series forecasting faces challenges due to co-evolving future variables under shared system dynamics, with existing models focusing mainly on historical cross-variable dependencies. Researchers identify a mismatch in the common Direct Forecasting approach, which uses point-wise objectives that do not constrain cross-variable structure in multi-step forecasts. To address this, they introduce Cross-Variable Loss (CvLoss), a structural regularizer that penalizes inconsistent residual differences across forecasted variables, encouraging consistency in both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Experiments demonstrate that CvLoss enhances competitive forecasting models, outperforms existing learning objectives, and integrates with various forecasting backbones.

item.title: Researchers propose Flow-JEPA, a flow-based latent dynamics model improving JEPA world model robustness to visual noise with up to 86% success under noisy conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Flow-JEPA (F-JEPA), a flow-based latent dynamics model designed to enhance Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) for latent world modeling and planning without reconstruction. F-JEPA generates sequences of future latent states conditioned on current observations and actions, using a Gaussian distribution as the flow source to transport perturbed latent trajectories toward clean future representations, shifting from pointwise transition regression to stochastic trajectory-level prediction. In experiments, F-JEPA increased mean success rates from 86% to 92% under clean observations and from 67% to 86% under noisy conditions, demonstrating improved robustness to localized, out-of-distribution visual noise. Further evaluations across varying perturbation severities and inference settings confirmed that F-JEPA's performance advantage persists broadly, suggesting conditional flow matching as a promising alternative to deterministic autoregressive prediction in JEPA world models.

item.title: Tail-Weight Control and Localized Generalization in Nearly Low-Rank Adversarial Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.23688v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Empirical ramp fitting can assign weight to pure-noise features even when the population optimum ignores them. We quantify this gap for norm-constrained adversarial classification with Gaussian signal and noise. The variance cost relative to normalized signed mean separates into two factors: selecting observations inside the active margin window and the curvature induced by the norm constraint. Changing the tail variance leaves the activewindow probability unchanged but changes the second factor. With positive attack budget and a signal-only predictor of risk below one half, we prove a uniform quadratic tail-deletion bound, including at zero tail variance. Sufficiently accurate approximate global empirical minimizers admit exact fixeddimensional asymptotic covariances in the low-risk regime with isotropic principal covariance. For positive tail variance at most principal variance, the product exceeds one; an additional moment condition transfers it to expected excess ramp and robust classification risks. A wide window analysis characterizes when this ordering reverses. Controlled experiments test the decomposition, and a separate contamination study examines its scope outside the Gaussian training model.

item.title: Which Self-Improvements Should We Trust? Reliable Self-Improvement When Agents Reuse Their Benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As recursive self-improvement (RSI) rapidly advances, reliable evaluation becomes critical for guiding adaptive search. RSI typically relies on finite evaluation resources, such as fixed benchmarks, to determine which modifications are retained and what is proposed next. However, when these finite resources are repeatedly reused, new candidates are proposed based on feedback from the same evaluation set, so the search trajectory can adaptively overfit and empirical improvement may not reflect genuine population improvement on the underlying task distribution. Some existing methods account for multiple comparisons but assume that candidates are chosen independently of the evaluation set, and therefore do not control this adaptive dependence. To address this, we propose REUSE (Risk-controlled Evaluation Under Sequential Evolution), a certified evaluation and promotion framework that allows a fixed evaluation set to support repeated adaptive decisions while providing statistical guarantees. For a user-specified error level $\alpha$, with probability at least $1-\alpha$, every promoted modification is a genuine population improvement on the underlying task distribution. REUSE achieves this by strictly limiting the evaluation feedback returned to the search process and accounting for possible promotion histories within the error budget. We develop detailed statistical theory for RSI evaluation in this setting, including simultaneous error control, valid lower bounds on cumulative improvement, and a characterization of the fundamental limits of adaptive evaluation reuse. In live self-improvement experiments, REUSE commits substantially fewer false promotions than evaluation frameworks from current RSI systems and error-controlled baselines, reducing the proportion of false promotions from up to 20.7% to 0%, while achieving final true population performance comparable to the best baselines.

item.title: Diffusion Reward Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models underpin the alignment of large language models, yet the dominant designs reduce each prompt--response pair to a point estimate or to a distribution from a fixed parametric family. This is at odds with human preference, which is inherently multimodal: the same response can be reasonably judged in many ways, and no single family covers all of them. To better fit this structure, we introduce DRM, a Diffusion Reward Model that recasts reward modeling as conditional density estimation over $p(\mathbf{r}\mid x,y)$. Conditioned on a frozen LLM encoder, a lightweight Diffusion Transformer denoises Gaussian noise into a reward vector, placing no parametric assumption on the output distribution and naturally representing its multimodal structure. A single architecture handles both multi-attribute regression and pairwise preference data, and at inference $N$ samples form an empirical reward distribution that can be aggregated into a scalar, a variance, or quantiles. Across five benchmarks, DRM matches or surpasses baselines under matched data and backbone, stays competitive with much larger discriminative, distributional, and generative RMs despite its modest training scale, and recovers multimodal reward structure where conventional heads collapse to a point. Uncertainty-aware rejection and lower-confidence-bound (LCB) aggregation further demonstrate that DRM can exploit distributional information beyond a scalar reward to improve reward-model decisions. Downstream RLHF experiments additionally show that using DRM as the training-time reward leads to improved policy performance, directly validating the practical benefit of diffusion-based reward modeling for RLHF training.

item.title: Counterfactual Rollout Replay: Forkable Environments as Free Process Rewards for Software Engineering Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33875v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Outcome-only reinforcement learning gives software engineering (SWE) agents a terminal success signal but little direct guidance about intermediate decisions. We introduce Counterfactual Rollout Replay (CRR), a training-time procedure that uses forkable executable environments to obtain step-level return contrasts. CRR selects a small set of decision points, restores each state, samples an alternative action, and rolls the branch forward under the policy. It retains the realised training trajectory and replaces the advantage at selected steps with the difference between its terminal return and the sampled counterfactual return. The method needs no human process labels or learned process reward model; free refers to those supervision costs, not replay compute. With a 14B policy, CRR improves pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live, and SWE-rebench, and combines with process-reward and trajectory-search methods. On SWE-bench Verified, an equal-wall-clock comparison on the same hardware yields 41.7% versus 36.7% for extended outcome-only GRPO, a 5.0-point gain with fork overhead included. These results apply to environments with affordable, reliable state restoration; stochastic continuations and expensive or imperfect replay remain limitations.

item.title: GradLev: Token-Parallel Test-Time Training Via Costate Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34174v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-time training (TTT) allows a model to improve its predictions at inference time by updating weights after every observed token. However, sequential gra- dient writes make parallel training difficult. We observe that, given layer inputs and activation gradients (costates), online gradient descent admits exact parallel scans for both forward evaluation and reverse backpropagation. GradLev lever- ages this duality: a causal auxiliary network predicts costates across all tokens in parallel; associative scans compute the adapted weights and forward activations and propagate gradients backward; and the resulting gradient targets supervise the predictor via a consistency loss. Exact consistency guarantees exact recovery of the sequential online learner. At deployment, the auxiliary predictor is discarded, and the model updates natively via token-by-token forward and backward passes.

item.title: LLMs are not stochastic parrots: Evidence for meaning-mediated abstraction from conlang-like tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34187v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The strong version of the stochastic parrot argument claims that, although large language models (LLMs) may exceed rote regurgitation, they cannot move beyond statistical pattern matching into abstraction or reasoning, remaining ontologically near the lower bound of pattern reuse despite producing alluringly fluent text. We test this hypothesis using conlang-like tasks. Several LLMs are given only natural-language descriptions of fictional languages that subvert prominent superficial patterns in training data by combining statistically uncommon and unattested features. Crucially, no example outputs are given. We argue that if the models exhibit rule-following behaviour, they cannot be relying solely on superficial statistical patterns; such patterns often work against the correct output. Instead, successful performance requires representations of the constraints specified in the prompt. Across three complementary task families, models systematically move in the meaning-predicted direction: they distinguish prompt exposure from instructed use, alter semantic relationships in response to novel constraints, and sometimes produce exact matches to complex translation answer keys. Although performance varies across the spectrum of models used, these results provide evidence for meaning-mediated abstraction in LLMs and refute the strong stochastic parrot hypothesis. Our work shows that, under appropriate architectural and contextual constraints, statistical learning can produce meaning-mediated abstractions, although generation remains strongly constrained by superficial plausibility. We discuss implications for model development and for understanding how increasingly abstract representations may emerge from plausible-text-generation objectives.

item.title: Coherence-Aware Distributional Evaluation of Open-Ended Text Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing open-ended generation metrics measure likelihood, lexical diversity, or distributional similarity in generic representation space, yet can miss fundamental dimensions of quality. A prominent blind spot is global coherence: a generated passage may be locally fluent while remaining globally contradictory, causally inconsistent, or topically disconnected. We identify representation as a central bottleneck in detecting these failures and introduce CHORD (Coherence-aware Hidden-state Open-generation Reference Distance), a coherence-sensitive distributional metric. CHORD encodes generated and human-written corpora in the hidden-state space of a frozen LLM using a coherence-eliciting prompt, and compares the resulting distributions using RBF-MMD. To test coherence sensitivity and selectivity, we construct a counterfactual evaluation suite pairing graded coherence-degrading perturbations with meaning-preserving controls. CHORD selectively detects relation, discourse, structural, and mixture failures that perplexity, entropy, MAUVE, FBD, and MMD-based baselines either miss or cannot separate from benign rewriting. Factorial ablations show that representation is the primary source of coherence sensitivity, while RBF-MMD improves sample efficiency. Larger backbones capture finer-grained distinctions, but coherence prompting improves selectivity only when the backbone can follow the prompt. On unconditional generation and prefix continuation, CHORD yields model rankings that strongly align with human judgments of whether outputs make sense and appear human-written. Together, these results establish representation design as central to reliable distributional evaluation. Code: https://github.com/MAPS-research/CHORD. Experiments: https://github.com/MAPS-research/CHORD-Experiment.

item.title: Don't Throw Away the Tail: Action Upcycling for Policy Acceleration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern robot policies predict a chunk of future actions from a single observation, execute only a prefix, and discard the rest before replanning. Choosing the length of this prefix, the execution horizon, poses a trade-off between reactivity and efficiency. A short horizon keeps the policy reactive to the environment, but requires frequent policy calls. Recent test-time methods adaptively select the horizon for each chunk, but they either read model internals, where the signal must be chosen for each architecture, or draw extra samples, which adds cost. We propose Action Upcycling, a training-free algorithm that reuses actions the policy would otherwise discard, without accessing model internals or drawing extra samples. We find that discarded actions stay close to their replanned versions as long as the action velocity remains smooth. Action Upcycling therefore extends the execution horizon up to the point where the velocity begins to fluctuate. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that Action Upcycling reduces policy calls by 1.2-1.7x with no loss in success rate, across multiple Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) and even a World Action Model (WAM). It applies to any chunked policy at negligible cost and is orthogonal to other policy acceleration methods such as few-step sampling and streaming action decoding, opening a new axis for policy acceleration.

item.title: Cyclostationary Phase Conditioning for Medical Time Series Diffusion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34965v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many physiological time series, such as cardiac and brain recordings, exhibit cyclostationarity: their statistics vary periodically with an underlying cycle phase. Corruption from motion, poor contact, and physiological interference obscures morphology needed for diagnosis, making signal restoration essential. Existing diffusion approaches condition on corrupted observations alone and must learn cyclic structure implicitly. We instead propose two inductive biases which encode cyclostationarity: a shift-covariant wavelet representation and dense per-sample phase conditioning inferred from the corrupted input. We further introduce a training-free cyclostationarity index that quantifies phase structure and predicts when phase conditioning will help. Finally, we propose antithetic coupling of reverse trajectories to reduce sampling variance while achieving comparable performance with fivefold fewer network evaluations. Across modalities, our results show that explicitly encoding measurable cyclic structure improves physiological time-series restoration.

item.title: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.35750v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling the horizon of agentic LLMs is bottlenecked by the need to fit ever longer context traces in GPU memory. Context compaction has been the most popular mechanism to alleviate this issue, keeping GPU memory constant for a given trace. Unfortunately, most compaction strategies rely on prefilling the LLM context many times over, hindering training throughput. To alleviate this bottleneck and enable efficient trainable compaction, we propose KV-streams, a plug-and-play strategy compatible with any compaction strategy that substantially increases throughput while showing no evidence of hindering performance. KV-streams enable scalable compaction by streaming the KV cache forward rather than flushing it after each compaction. We show that KV-streams enable three different compaction strategies, achieving a 2.6 to 5x wall-clock speedup in training. Beyond efficiency, we find that the streamed KV cache can act as a recurrent state, carrying forward information that has long since disappeared from the context. Specifically, in a controlled setting we show that, contrary to prior work, RL alone is all that is needed for this behavior to emerge. Overall, we show KV-streams to be an efficient and lightweight plug-and-play addition to any post-training pipeline.

item.title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.35760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) agent executes the same task, token consumption can vary by over an order of magnitude across runs. The agent chooses its next steps based on tool feedback and intermediate results, while the growing context steadily inflates the input size of every subsequent call. The total consumption of a task is therefore hard to predict before execution and the prediction must be revised as the run unfolds. In this paper, we propose TokenCast, which learns a composable cost representation for each execution segment, recording its own consumption and the context growth it introduces. Composing adjacent segments yields a cumulative estimate that captures the extra input cost incurred when context from earlier segments is re-read by every later call. As execution unfolds, newly observed evidence refreshes the forecast, requiring no additional LLM calls and incurring a mean cumulative prediction time of 32.8 ms per run on SWE-bench Verified. Across 4 task suites and 6 agent models, TokenCast's mean absolute error reduction against the strongest comparator averages 14.5% over 96 evaluated combinations. In offline budget-control replay, TokenCast uses 21.3% fewer tokens on average than a fixed-budget policy at matched trace completion. The code is available at https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/TokenCast.
